Jaumann absorbers consist of multiple resistive layers separated by quarter-wavelength low-loss spacers in front of a metal backing sheet.
The design problem is N-dimensional, involving optimization of sheet resistances and spacer properties over frequency, polarization, and angle.
Genetic algorithms do not require derivatives of the performance function and are robust against local optima.
Bandwidth increases rapidly with the number of resistive layers N up to about 7-8 layers, then approaches an asymptotic limit.
Adding a low-permittivity dielectric spacer (εr=1.1) in front of the outermost resistive layer marginally improves bandwidth.
The GA-optimized sheet resistance profile is S-shaped, differing from the traditional exponential profile by flattening at outer layers.
Typical optimized sheet resistance values for a 7-layer absorber with εr=1.1 range from ~2163 Ω/sq (innermost) to ~430 Ω/sq (outermost).
Reflectivity performance is evaluated over 1-20 GHz with a target of -20 dB or better reflectivity.
A two-stage GA performance function first minimizes reflectivity peaks above -20 dB, then maximizes the -20 dB bandwidth.
Floating-point gene representation in GA improves execution speed compared to binary encoding.
Oblique incidence degrades RAM performance and introduces polarization sensitivity; GA optimization can target equal bandwidth for both polarizations.
Adding a high-permittivity skin (e.g., fiber-reinforced plastic with εr=4) can degrade performance but re-optimization recovers bandwidth.
Active Jaumann absorbers can dynamically vary sheet resistance, spacer thickness, or permittivity to achieve frequency-agile reflectivity.
Varying sheet resistances controls reflectivity null amplitudes symmetrically about the center frequency.
Varying spacer thicknesses allows asymmetric tuning of reflectivity nulls and creation of broadband nulls with spot nulls at selected frequencies.
For a single-layer Salisbury screen (N=1), the optimized sheet resistance is about 369 Ω/sq instead of the classical 377 Ω/sq.
GA-optimized absorbers with N=12 layers achieve bandwidths around 1.8 (normalized units) at -20 dB reflectivity.
The presence of a dielectric front spacer or skin can be used to protect mechanical integrity or form part of electromagnetic matching.
The GA approach can reduce design size significantly (up to 68%) while maintaining or improving absorption performance.
Reflectivity nulls can be dynamically reconfigured in active RAM for subband performance at the expense of broadband performance.
